introduction-you-are-spending-money.core: Engineers allocate capital with every terraform apply, storage choice or rewrite. Thinking in money (cost, return, opportunity) makes engineering decisions better and more persuasive.

first_principles.problem: A single command can provision more cost per month than an employee's salary, and a 'quick rewrite in Rust' can burn $250k of engineering time, yet engineers rarely think in those terms.

analogy.title: A company credit card
analogy.story: You've been handed a card with no limit. Every purchase is real money, even if no one asks you to justify it.
analogy.breaks: Credit cards show purchases immediately. Engineering time costs are invisible unless you estimate them.

example.title: The Rust rewrite
example.scenario: A team proposes rewriting a stable service in Rust.

steps.label: Economics
steps.detail: 25-year payback; the rewrite is a hobby, not an investment.

example.outcome: the decision is made on value, not excitement.

check.q: What's often the biggest hidden cost in engineering decisions?

total-cost-of-ownership-tco.core: Total cost of ownership counts every cost over a system's life: licences or cloud, people to build and run it, training, migration, downtime and eventual decommissioning, not just the sticker price.

first_principles.problem: Self-hosting looks cheaper than a managed service until you add the engineers who patch, monitor and get paged for it.
truths: Running costs exceed build costs over time.
derivation: Compare options on TCO, not price.

analogy.title: Owning a car
analogy.story: The $30k sticker price becomes $55k over five years with fuel, insurance, repairs and depreciation.
analogy.breaks: Car costs are predictable. Software TCO includes uncertain items like incidents, so estimate ranges.

example.title: Self-hosted Kafka vs managed

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Half an engineer's time outweighs the infra savings.

example.outcome: the cheaper-looking option turns out to cost more.

check.a: Ongoing people time: maintenance, upgrades and on-call.

capex-vs-opex-mental-models.core: CAPEX is upfront spending on long-lived assets (depreciated over years); OPEX is ongoing expense (cloud bills, subscriptions). Finance treats them differently, so frame proposals accordingly.

first_principles.problem: Engineers propose 'move to cloud' or 'buy servers' purely on totals, and finance rejects or delays them for reasons engineers don't understand.
truths: Some budgets are CAPEX-only or OPEX-only.
derivation: **CAPEX**: buy servers, build a platform (capitalised dev time), depreciated.
Frame the proposal in **that budget's terms**.

analogy.title: Buying vs renting a house
analogy.story: Buying is a big upfront cost spread over years (CAPEX); renting is a monthly bill you can stop (OPEX).
analogy.breaks: Housing rules are simple. Accounting rules vary by company and country, so ask finance.

example.title: On-prem GPUs vs cloud GPUs

steps.label: Framing
steps.detail: Same compute, but the CAPEX framing matched the open budget.

example.outcome: the proposal is approved because it speaks finance's language.

check.q: Is cloud spend usually CAPEX or OPEX?

opportunity-cost-in-build-vs-buy.core: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you gave up. Building in-house costs not just salaries but the product features those engineers didn't ship.

first_principles.problem: A team builds a custom feature-flag system 'because it's only 3 months'. Those 3 months could have shipped a feature worth far more.
truths: Every 'yes' is a 'no' to something else.
Opportunity cost isn't on any invoice.
derivation: Ask: **what else would these people build?**
Include it in **build vs buy** comparisons.

analogy.title: Mowing your own lawn
analogy.story: A lawyer billing $400/hour who spends 3 hours mowing has an opportunity cost of $1,200, far more than hiring someone.
analogy.breaks: Hourly rates are known. The value of unbuilt features is estimated, so use ranges.

example.title: Custom feature-flag system

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: The delayed revenue dwarfs the build cost itself.

example.outcome: the team ships the revenue feature and buys the tool.

check.q: Why is opportunity cost often the largest cost?
check.a: Because the value of product work forgone usually exceeds the direct cost of building the tool.

the-cost-of-coordination-brookss-law.core: Adding people to a late project makes it later (Brooks's law): new people need ramp-up, and communication paths grow as n(n−1)/2, so coordination overhead outpaces added capacity.

first_principles.problem: A project is behind, so management adds five engineers. Velocity drops for two months as veterans onboard newcomers and meetings multiply.
truths: New people take time to become productive.
derivation: Expect a **ramp-up dip** when adding people.
Prefer **small, autonomous teams** with clear interfaces.
Reduce scope rather than add people late.

analogy.title: Nine women can't make a baby in one month
analogy.story: Some work has inherent sequence; more people don't shorten it.
analogy.breaks: Pregnancy can't be split at all. Much software work can, if architecture allows independent teams.

example.title: Rescuing a late launch

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: Ship a smaller first version on time.

example.outcome: the launch lands without the coordination collapse.

check.q: How many communication paths does a 10-person team have?

unit-economics-for-infrastructure.core: Total cost doesn't tell you if spending is healthy; cost per unit of value does (cost per order, per active user, per GB processed). Track it over time to see whether you scale efficiently.

first_principles.problem: A $100k/month bill might be great for a company processing $50M, or terrible for one processing $50k. Without a ratio, nobody knows.
truths: Cost should scale with value delivered.
Business units are what leaders track.
derivation: Choose a **unit** that matches what the business sells (orders, users, API calls).
Track the **trend**: rising per-unit cost means waste.

analogy.title: Fuel economy
analogy.story: Total fuel bought means little; litres per 100 km tells you if the car is efficient.
analogy.breaks: Fuel economy has one unit. Platforms may need several units per product line.

example.title: Cost per order

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: Logging volume grew faster than orders.

example.outcome: the business sees whether growth is efficient.

check.q: Why is cost per unit better than total cost?
check.a: It shows whether spend scales efficiently with the value delivered.

finops-engineering-meets-finance.core: FinOps makes cloud spending a shared responsibility: engineers see their costs, finance understands drivers, and teams continuously inform, optimise and operate spending.

first_principles.problem: In the cloud, anyone can spend money with one command, but nobody sees the bill until month end, and nobody owns it.
derivation: **Inform**: tag resources, show cost per team.
Make it **cultural**, not a finance audit.

analogy.title: Splitting a household electricity bill
analogy.story: When each flatmate sees their own usage, the heater gets turned off; one shared bill nobody sees leads to waste.
analogy.breaks: Electricity is simple. Cloud pricing is complex, so FinOps needs tooling and expertise.

example.title: Per-team cost dashboards
example.scenario: A company's cloud bill grows 40% a year.

check.q: What are the three FinOps phases?
